text: I persuaded Bay Ganyo to take a walk to the opera and get tickets for the evening. They were performing the ballet "Puppenfee" and I don't remember what else. We passed the Greek café, turned toward Café Mendl, where the Bulgarians gather, and headed toward St. Stephen's Cathedral. Here on the square, I invited Bay Ganyo to stop by a pastry shop, not suspecting that the character of Don Juan could get under Bay Ganyo's skin. But what wonders civilization can work! I should tell you that I was studying in Vienna then; I had gone home for the holidays and was returning now, so on the way to Vienna, I met Bay Ganyo. I used to go to this pastry shop often and knew the cashier very well, a pretty and cheerful girl—cheerful, but she conducted herself well and did not allow any liberties. And imagine, gentlemen, Bay Ganyo and I enter the pastry shop, we approach the counter, the girl greets me cheerfully with a welcome, I reply with some playful pleasantries and turn back to choose something sweet, and at that moment an indignant shriek deafened the whole establishment...
– What happened, Bay Ganyo, did you do something to her? – I shouted anxiously and angrily.
– I didn't, brother, what have I done to her – Bay Ganyo answered haltingly with a trembling voice.

The girl, extremely angry, with a flushed face, told me in a loud voice that Bay Ganyo had insulted her by deed, had grabbed her, and not only grabbed her, but even twisted his hand with clenched teeth. She wanted to call the policeman. Scandal!

– Get out of here quickly, Bai Ganyo; if the policeman catches you, you're done for; go on up, I'll catch up with you – I shouted with feigned indignation and almost burst out laughing as I looked at the tragicomic figure of Bai Ganyo.

– Why is she putting on airs! – said Bay Ganyo boldly as he was leaving. – As if she’s so virtuous? I know the women around here. Show her the purse – and suddenly it’s "gut morgen," but your old Bay Ganyo isn't a fool!...

It was fated that I should conclude the day's impressions with one more adventure, the hero of which was again our Bai Ganyo. At the opera, as I told you, they were performing the ballet "Puppenfee." We occupied seats in the parterre. The theater was full. Bai Ganyo’s grayish-brown clothes stood out in sharp contrast against the general dark background of the suits. The curtain rose. Silence—deadly. Everyone had their eyes fixed on the fantastically decorated stage. I felt that on my right side Bai Ganyo was fidgeting and puffing, but I could not tear my eyes away from the stage: the scenes of the ballet were constantly changing at the movement of a magic wand; various groups of ballerinas appeared and disappeared; on the stage, now darkness, now monochromatic, now multicolored light—a phantasmagoria! From the general group of ballerinas, one detached herself, stepped with small quick steps toward the forestage, stopped, leaped, and floated through the air, supported only on the tip of one foot... At that very moment, behind my back, a hysterical ha-ha-ha-ha! split the air. I turned to the left—all the rows behind me were giggling and pointing at something on my right side. Instantly, a foreboding thought crossed my mind. I turned toward Bai Ganyo... My God! What do I see! Bai Ganyo had stripped down to his shirt sleeves and unbuttoned his vest, which was tight on him from the vials stuffed into his sash: one of the theater attendants had caught him by the sleeve with two fingers and was making quite unambiguous signs with his head for him to step outside; Bai Ganyo stared back at him and replied also with signs—as if to say, "Who do you think you're scaring?" It was this very "tough guy" moment that elicited hysterical laughter from a little girl sitting behind us, and this laughter infected the whole theater. What a scene! And imagine, gentlemen, I looked, sinking with shame, toward the boxes—as if someone were pulling me to look—and my eyes met the fixed gaze of an entire familiar German family, in whose home I was very well received, and in their eyes I read sincere pity for my desperate situation. And meanwhile, Bai Ganyo was pulling me energetically by the sleeve:
– Come on, let's get out of here, leave those kikes alone – I'll get my hands on them, just you wait!...
